extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in history, political philosophy, and the causes of social progress
extracted.subtask_description: An essay-level discussion of why some societies progress while others remain stationary, arguing that institutions of discussion, tolerance, and certain social structures produce cultural advance. Covers causes (war, migration, custom), institutions (discussion, caste, priesthood), and psychological/sociological mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government by discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress arises when government operates by discussion — where sovereign power is divided among many persons and important matters are openly debated (a 'government by discussion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues this is the crucial change from the 'age of status' to the 'age of choice': putting subjects up to discussion admits they are not settled by custom, dissolves the sacred charm of use and wont, and makes them permanently open to free choice. Examples cited: Athens, small Greek and Italian republics, medieval communes and states-general. Once a subject is submitted to public deliberation it cannot be re-consecrated or withdrawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of topics debated (principles vs transactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion must concern abstract or principled subjects (matters of principle) rather than merely isolated practical transactions to produce lasting emancipation from custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debates limited to expeditions or village choices (typical of many tribal/oratory cultures) sharpen oratorical skill but do not encourage speculative intellect or challenge entrenched usage. Only discussion of general political principles breaks the yoke of custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance as a precondition and product of discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolerance is both required for, and learned through, sustained public discussion; a society that cannot endure opposing views cannot sustain productive discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful discussion presumes an ability to hear unpleasant ideas without 'howling them down.' Tolerance is presented as the modern idea that allows different beliefs to coexist without harming others; anti-patterns include assemblies where dissenters are shouted down (example: certain French assemblies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives to intelligence and argumentative skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Government by discussion creates a premium for argumentative intelligence: producing persuasive political arguments is rewarded and thus fosters intellectual development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because political discussion must move those who act within the bounds of contemporary ideas and precedents, good reasoning is favored; this selection for argumentative skill encourages the growth of vigorous thinkers and, indirectly, broader cultural advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex polity/constitutional structure enabling factional debate
rubrics_metrics.description: A polity with distinct organs or parties (e.g., monarch, senate, general meeting/citizens) enables sustained debate on principles and the emergence of political controversy that propels change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Greek city-states where aristocratic senates and popular assemblies clashed, producing principle-based controversies. The existence of competing parties/factions encourages discussion of foundational questions rather than only transactional choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixity of custom as stabilizer and impediment
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed customary law provides essential order in early societies but simultaneously arrests onward progress — custom binds people into immutable practices and discourages individual originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay explains that in early ages law 'rested on status' and was felt as sacred; deviation was often punished as religious impiety. While necessary to coerce order in fledgling societies, this fixity explains widespread historical stagnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness or quality of subjects under discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: The cultural impact of discussion depends on the importance of the topics debated; when 'great ideas are in the air' (e.g., Reformation, geographic discovery), discussion propels broad flourishing in arts and sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Elizabethan England — discussion on religion and discovery correlated with strides in poetry (Shakespeare), prose (Bacon), architecture and scientific reform. Periods with high-quality public topics encourage originality across domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner and ceremonial dignity as social glue
rubrics_metrics.description: In customary societies, an impressive, dignified manner and finely regulated ceremonies are central means of maintaining obedience to custom and social hierarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed examples (Persian court etiquette, the ritualized offering of coffee and pipes) illustrate how minute ceremonial norms enforce rank and encourage conformity; 'manner' is both auxiliary and principal in imposing custom in early societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of customs through group isolation and migration
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom-making is facilitated by societal divisions, migrations, and lack of long-range communication — as groups separate, dialects and customs diverge and new, binding usages emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that early migrations created isolated groups whose speech and practices quickly diverged; lack of written literature and intercourse meant separate groups 'set up house' and produced distinct persistent characters and customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wars and conflict as regenerators of society
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent wars and conflicts fracture old images and introduce new elements, serving as engines of social regeneration and preventing stagnation from single customs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text characterizes constant conflict as a source of continual infusion of new elements into society, breaking monotonies and enabling new formations of custom and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection (conscious or unconscious) shaping national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Both unconscious natural selection and social/cultural selection (e.g., survival in harsh regimes) produce 'breeds' or national characters over time; societies tend to eliminate ill-fitted individuals and thus consolidate dominant traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues that rigid customary societies implicitly select for conformist, hardy types (Spartan example). Mr. Galton's idea of deliberate mating is seen as a modern parallel to long-run natural processes in primitive societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caste/composite societies: short-term advantage, long-term impediment
rubrics_metrics.description: Caste or composite societies (many tribes/castes bound together) have an early advantage because their internal diversity at the national level provides cooperative contrast (e.g., warrior and priest castes), but each caste's internal monotony tends to arrest long-term progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: protection for an intellectual class (priests), combined martial defence (warrior castes), national durability. Disadvantages: each caste develops indelible, invariable shades; collectively the nation may last long but cease to progress, often 'stopping early.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Atavism and instability under sudden choice
rubrics_metrics.description: When repression of passions enforced by custom is suddenly removed (e.g., revolution or riot), societies can revert ('atavism') to unstable, barbarous behaviors; inherited passions re-emerge and can produce cruelty and disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: French Revolution and riots where suppressed impulses break out; explanation: people originally unable to 'look steadily' to long-term ends become highly excitable when freed from habitual restraint.
